title: The Macroeconomic Consequences of Undermining Central Bank Independence: Evidence from Governor Transitions (Working Paper 2026/040)
key_claim: Leveraging a new panel dataset covering 132 central bank governor transitions in 28 advanced and emerging market economies since 2000, the paper finds that tenures of governors with politically motivated appointments are associated with higher and more volatile inflation, realised and expected; following a politically motivated transition, nominal and real short rates decline while expected and realised inflation rise and GDP growth temporarily increases; long-term inflation expectations rise in the case of unorthodox governors, indicating pronounced costs to central bank credibility.
frame_summary: The IMF presents primary evidence that political interference in central bank leadership systematically raises inflation and erodes credibility, even where formal independence exists.
notes: Tier 1 IMF primary research. Structural anchor (3-6m band) for the macro-consequences framing; cited inline like any other source.

title: The quiet erosion of central bank independence (speech by Isabel Schnabel)
date_evidence: London, 7 May 2026 ; Speech by Isabel Schnabel, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the Fifth Annual Charles Goodhart Lecture
key_claim: ECB Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel argues central bank independence is at risk from direct political attacks (citing the 'legal attacks' on the Federal Reserve) and from two structural forces quietly eroding it: fiscal dominance (rising government debt) and financial dominance; she notes that by early 2025 hedge funds' share of secondary-market trading had risen to around one-third in US Treasuries and higher in euro-area sovereign bonds, and that while in March the median euro-area consumer expected three-year-ahead inflation of 3%, market-based longer-term inflation expectations remain anchored around the 2% target.
frame_summary: Schnabel argues that political pressure plus fiscal and financial dominance are quietly eroding the conditions for independent monetary policy, threatening the anchor for long-term inflation expectations.
notes: Tier 1 ECB speech. Provides the euro-area / global framing and the counter-point that market-based long-term expectations remain anchored.

title: World Economic Outlook, April 2026: Global Economy in the Shadow of War
date_evidence: World Economic Outlook, April 2026: Global Economy in the Shadow of War (https://www.imf.org/en/publications/weo/issues/2026/04/14/world-economic-outlook-april-2026)
key_claim: The April 2026 WEO warns that an erosion of institutions, including central bank independence and monetary policy credibility, could raise inflation expectations, especially while headline inflation is rising; reanchoring expectations usually requires a prolonged period of tight monetary policy, with longer-term yields rising on widening term premiums and higher inflation expectations, ultimately lowering economic growth; global growth is projected to slow to 3.1 percent in 2026.
frame_summary: The IMF's flagship outlook flags political pressure on independent institutions as a key downside risk that could lift inflation expectations and lower growth.
notes: Tier 1 IMF flagship. URL carries publication date 2026/04/14. Macro risk framing.

title: Challenges to independence: How should central banks respond - lessons from history (speech by Donald Kohn)
date_evidence: May 27, 2026 ; A speech given by Don Kohn at a Bank of Japan-hosted conference in May 2026 (2026 BOJ-IMES Conference, held on May 27 and 28)
key_claim: Former Federal Reserve Vice Chair Donald Kohn argues that threats to central bank independence have risen sharply in the United States, to levels not seen since the Fed-Treasury accord of 1951, that concerns are broader than the US, and that preserving independence has become among the defining institutional challenges of the moment.
frame_summary: Kohn, drawing on history, argues that US central bank independence is under its most serious threat since 1951 and that central banks must defend it.
notes: Tier 2 think tank (Brookings), former Fed Vice Chair. Historical-comparison anchor for the severity of the current threat.

title: Will the Federal Reserve remain independent? (interview with Daniel Tarullo)
date_evidence: Jan 15, 2026 ; Harvard Law Professor Daniel Tarullo argues that, in the upcoming Supreme Court case Trump v. Cook, 'the independence of the Federal Reserve is really at stake'
key_claim: Former Fed Governor and Harvard Law professor Daniel Tarullo explains that beginning about 15 years ago the Supreme Court began narrowing the for-cause removal protection that, since the 90-year-old 1935 Humphrey's Executor precedent, insulated independent-agency heads; he expects the Court to overturn or severely limit Humphrey's while possibly carving out the Federal Reserve as 'different', and warns that if markets become convinced the Fed operates as a subsidiary of the administration, longer-term interest rates could rise significantly, reducing US growth potential.
frame_summary: Tarullo argues the Court is likely to gut Humphrey's Executor (perhaps sparing the Fed) and that losing Fed independence would push up long-term rates and lower growth.
notes: Tier 2 academic (Harvard Law). In the 3-6m band; not flagged as the single structural anchor (IMF WP 2026/040 holds that role) but used inline for the legal mechanism, the Fed carve-out, and the counter-argument. Dated Jan 15 2026, within the audit's 180-day window.

title: The Supreme Court is in its final stretch this term. Here are the major cases left
key_claim: As of early-to-mid June 2026 the Supreme Court has not yet decided Trump v. Slaughter (FTC) or Trump v. Cook (Federal Reserve), with rulings expected by the end of June or early July; since the 1935 Humphrey's Executor decision (which limited removal of commissioners to 'inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance'), every Court has reaffirmed it, but the six conservative justices are widely expected to rule in the president's favour, the result being that independent agencies will no longer be independent, while some justices have suggested the Federal Reserve may have more protection than other agencies.
frame_summary: NPR reports that the Court is poised to expand presidential power to fire independent-agency heads, likely ending agency independence while possibly treating the Fed differently.
notes: Tier 3 quality journalism (Nina Totenberg). In-window source confirming the pending status and likely direction of the rulings. Updated 12 June 2026.

title: How Trump's repeated efforts to fire the Federal Reserve chair harm the economy
date_evidence: meta-article:published_time: 2026-04-17T09:40:25+00:00 ; by Ana Carolina Garriga, Cristina Bodea
key_claim: Political-economy scholars argue that President Trump's threats to oust Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell and his move to fire Governor Lisa Cook put central bank independence at risk; markets typically react to such threats by pricing in higher future inflation, driving up longer-term interest rates, whereas an independent central bank gives markets confidence that inflation will be lower and more stable, reducing the term premium.
frame_summary: The authors argue that attacks on Fed leadership raise inflation expectations and long-term borrowing costs, harming the economy.
notes: Tier 3 republished academic commentary (originally The Conversation; authors Garriga and Bodea). Source for the market/term-premium transmission channel.
